units.text: Start at the upper-left warmup clock. Default instance warmup controls when newly in-service instances contribute to aggregate utilization metrics, helping the scaling controller avoid misleading startup measurements.
Move to the upper-right shield. A health-check grace period delays certain replacement decisions during startup. It is not an application readiness test and should not replace one.
Look at the prepared instances in the lower-left pool. A warm pool can shorten startup delay, but its stopped, running or hibernated configuration changes cost and retained state.

Follow the lower-right initialization checklist. Use lifecycle hooks to finish bootstrap work before proceeding, and test restored instances before they serve traffic. Prepared infrastructure can still have unavailable dependencies.

With the whole slide visible, keep these controls separate. Measure initialization and readiness, then configure each mechanism for its own purpose. One timer cannot prove that an application is ready.
Begin with the blue launch path on the left. A launch hook gives initialization, validation or registration automation a bounded wait before the instance proceeds into service.
Compare the purple termination path on the right. During normal termination, a hook can provide time for draining, log collection and cleanup. Design the work to complete within its allowed interval.

Follow the heartbeat panel below. Automation must report progress or complete the lifecycle action. Choose timeout and failure outcomes explicitly, because waiting is bounded and failure handling is part of the design.
Inspect the interruption warning. A lifecycle hook cannot prevent Spot capacity interruption or every sudden failure. Keep important state durable, and make cleanup bounded and safe to retry.
With the full diagram restored, trace both directions. Launch work establishes readiness; termination work reduces disruption. Test the failure paths as carefully as the successful pauses.

Start with the launch-template panel on the left. For the rolling replacement shown here, specify the desired template version and start instance refresh. Editing a template alone does not replace the existing fleet.

Move to the healthy-capacity panel. Minimum and maximum healthy percentages constrain replacement batches, while warmup accounts for initialization. Check actual serving capacity as instances are replaced.

Follow the checkpoint and alarm path below. Checkpoints pause progress, and bake time provides a final observation period. Enable supported automatic rollback if failures or configured alarms should reverse the deployment.

Inspect the compatibility checklist on the right. Rollback requires a supported previous configuration, including a specific numbered launch-template version. Replacing instances does not undo a database migration or restore application data.

With the whole slide visible, follow the complete rollout. Validate the new version, observe real application health, and retain a tested recovery plan. Compute replacement and data recovery remain separate responsibilities.
